request.system:
You review a blog article an online shop is about to publish. You did not write it. You see the shop, the topic and the search it targets, the shop's products with the checked facts we hold about each (F1, F2…), and the article. Sentences about products end with the facts they rest on in brackets; [G] marks a sentence the writer says is general knowledge.

Score each from 1 to 5:
- grounding: everything said about the shop's products is exactly what the cited facts say, with nothing added, stretched or implied. One product claim the facts do not support caps this at 2. No invented experience ("we tested", customer stories), statistics or studies.
- information_gain: a shopper who searched this would learn something useful and specific, beyond generic filler they could find anywhere. Padding, repetition and vague praise lower it.
- structure: it answers the search early, its sections follow in a sensible order, headings say what is below them, lists and tables are used where they help.
- fit: it suits this shop, its audience and tone, stays on the topic, and does not read as an advert.
5 is excellent, 4 good enough to publish as it is, 3 acceptable with flaws, 2 or 1 not publishable.

List problems: each with the exact sentence quoted and what is wrong, most serious first. Leave the list empty if there are none.

For each numbered general-knowledge sentence you are given, say whether every number in it is well established and uncontroversial general knowledge that needs no source (accepted true), or not (false), with a short reason.

<article>
Title: How to Make Cold Brew Coffee at Home: Ratio, Grind and Steep Time

To make cold brew coffee, steep coarsely ground coffee in cold water in the fridge for many hours, strain out the grounds, then dilute the concentrate to taste. A reliable starting point for concentrate is about 1 part coffee to 10 parts water by weight [G]. Grind coarse, weigh both coffee and water, and give it time. This guide covers the ratio, grind size and steep time, a step-by-step method in a dedicated jar or a French press, and how to choose beans and serve the result.

## What cold brew is, and why time replaces heat

Cold brew is an immersion method: the grounds sit fully submerged in water for the whole brew, rather than having water pass through them as in pour-over. The difference is temperature. Hot brewing water usually sits around 90 to 96 °C and extracts flavour in a few minutes [G]. Cold water extracts far more slowly, so time has to do the work that heat normally does.

That slow, cold extraction pulls out less of the sharp acids and bitter compounds that hot water dissolves readily. The result is a smooth, rounded, low-bitterness concentrate. Our [Cold Brew Jar](P1) is an immersion brewer built for exactly this, with a recommended steep of 12 to 18 hours in the fridge [F2, F10].

Cold brew is not the same as iced coffee. Iced coffee is brewed hot and then cooled or poured over ice, so it keeps the brightness and aromatics of a hot brew. Cold brew never sees heat, which is why it tastes heavier, sweeter and softer.

## What you need

The kit is simple, but each piece matters:

- **A vessel with a filter.** Anything that lets you steep and then separate the grounds cleanly will work.
- **A burr grinder that grinds coarse.** Burrs give a more even particle size than blades, which keeps the brew clean.
- **A scale.** Ratio is everything in cold brew, and weighing is far more consistent than scooping.
- **Cold, filtered water.** Water makes up most of the drink, so off-tastes in the tap water carry straight through.
- **Fresh beans.** Coffee ground just before brewing gives a fuller, sweeter concentrate.

If you want a dedicated brewer, our Cold Brew Jar is a 1.5 litre glass jar made by Fernhill, with a fine stainless steel filter basket and an airtight lid [F1, F3, F4, F5, F8]. The basket keeps the grounds contained during the steep and lifts out when the brew is done [F5].

{{P1}}

You can browse the rest of our [immersion brewers](L3) if you would rather use a vessel that also handles hot brewing.

## Ratio and grind size

### The ratio

For a concentrate, aim for roughly 1:10 coffee to water by weight [G]. In the Cold Brew Jar, that means filling the basket with up to 150 g of coarse ground coffee to make 1.5 litres of concentrate [F6, F7]. If you prefer a ready-to-drink brew rather than a concentrate, use less coffee for the same amount of water and skip most of the dilution later.

### The grind

Grind coarse, at roughly the size you would use for a French press. A coarse grind lets water move freely between the particles and extract evenly over the long steep. Fine particles, often called fines, cause two problems: they over-extract and add bitterness, and they slip through filters and make the concentrate muddy. An even, coarse grind is the single biggest factor in a clean cold brew.

Our [Hand Grinder](P3) has external click adjustment with 30 settings, running from espresso to French press [F26, F27]. It grinds with 38 mm hardened stainless steel conical burrs [F25]. It holds 25 g of beans at a time, so a full 150 g basket means grinding in several loads [F28, F6].

{{P3}}

If you brew large batches often, an electric grinder saves effort; see our full range of [grinders](L1).

## Step by step: making cold brew in the jar

1. **Weigh and grind the coffee.** Weigh your beans, then grind them coarse, just before brewing.
2. **Fill the filter basket.** Put the grounds into the Cold Brew Jar's fine stainless steel basket [F5].
3. **Pour cold water slowly.** Add cold, filtered water gradually so every ground is wetted. Dry pockets extract poorly, so give the slurry a gentle stir if any grounds stay dry.
4. **Seal and refrigerate.** Close the airtight lid and put the jar in the fridge; it fits in a fridge door [F8, F9].
5. **Steep for 12 to 18 hours.** This is the recommended steep time for the Cold Brew Jar in the fridge [F10].
6. **Lift out the basket and let it drain.** Hold the basket over the jar until the dripping slows, then remove it. Avoid squeezing or pressing the wet grounds, which pushes fines and bitterness into the concentrate.

Within the recommended window, steep time is your main tuning tool. A shorter steep gives a brighter, lighter brew; a longer steep gives a heavier, more chocolate-led one. Change one thing at a time between batches so you know what made the difference.

## No dedicated jar? Using a French press

A French press works well for cold brew because it is already an immersion brewer with a built-in filter. The method is the same: add coarse coffee, pour in cold water, stir to wet everything, put the lid on without pressing, and steep in the fridge. When it is ready, press the plunger down slowly and decant the coffee into a separate bottle straight away, so the liquid stops sitting on the grounds and over-extracting.

Our French Press holds 1 litre and filters with a four-layer mesh [F52, F58]. Because it is an immersion brewer, it suits cold brew without any extra parts [F53]. Keep the same ratio and scale it down: at 1:10, a litre of water takes about 100 g of coffee [G]. A mesh filter lets a little more sediment through than a fine basket, so a coarse, even grind matters even more here.

## Choosing beans for cold brew

Cold extraction tends to mute acidity and push sweetness, body and chocolate notes forward. That makes medium roasts with caramel and chocolate character a dependable choice; they taste rich and rounded without turning flat.

[Colombia Huila](P2) is a strong match: it is a washed, single-origin medium roast with tasting notes of red apple, caramel and milk chocolate [F11, F15, F20, F22]. It comes in 250 g and 1 kg bags, and the larger bag suits anyone brewing full jars regularly [F14].

{{P2}}

Fruit-forward light roasts also work if you want a brighter, more aromatic glass. Our Ethiopia Guji, for example, is a natural-process light roast with notes of blueberry, dark chocolate and jasmine [F40, F41, F42]. Expect cold brewing to soften its acidity while keeping the fruit. You can compare origins across our [coffee beans](L2) collection.

## Diluting, serving and storing

### Diluting and serving

A full Cold Brew Jar batch is concentrate, not a ready-to-drink coffee [F7]. Start by diluting it about 1:1 with cold water or milk over ice, then adjust to taste [G]. Some simple ways to serve it:

- **Black over ice** with cold water, for the cleanest taste of the bean.
- **With milk or a plant milk**, which suits chocolate-led coffees particularly well.
- **Topped up with sparkling water** for a lighter, brighter drink.
- **Diluted with hot water** if you want a quick, low-bitterness hot coffee.

### Storing

Keep the concentrate sealed and cold, and use it within about a week, since flavour fades and turns stale over time. With the basket removed, the concentrate can stay in the jar with the airtight lid closed, in the fridge door [F8, F9]. A clean glass bottle with a tight cap works just as well if you need the jar for the next batch.

### Troubleshooting a batch

| Problem | Likely cause | What to change |
|---|---|---|
| Sour, thin or watery | Under-extraction | Grind a little finer, steep longer, or use more coffee |
| Bitter or harsh | Over-extraction or too many fines | Grind coarser, shorten the steep, and do not squeeze the grounds |
| Muddy or gritty | Fines passing the filter | Grind coarser and more evenly, and decant carefully |
| Weak once diluted | Too much dilution | Dilute less, or brew a stronger concentrate |

Make one change per batch and note your ratio, grind setting and steep time. After two or three batches you will have a recipe that suits your beans and your taste, and cold brew becomes one of the most forgiving ways to brew at home.
</article>
